  (declName : Lean.Name) :
  [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if the environment contains a declaration with name `declName`

def

```lean
[Lean.Macro.getCurrNamespace]](#manual-Lean___Macro___getCurrNamespace) : [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) Lean.Name



[Lean.Macro.getCurrNamespace]](#manual-Lean___Macro___getCurrNamespace) :
  [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) Lean.Name
```

Gets the current namespace given the position in the file.

def

```lean
[Lean.Macro.resolveNamespace]](#manual-Lean___Macro___resolveNamespace) (n : Lean.Name) :
  [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([List]](#manual-List___nil) Lean.Name)



[Lean.Macro.resolveNamespace]](#manual-Lean___Macro___resolveNamespace)
  (n : Lean.Name) :
  [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([List]](#manual-List___nil) Lean.Name)
```

Resolves the given name to an overload list of namespaces.

def

```lean
[Lean.Macro.resolveGlobalName]](#manual-Lean___Macro___resolveGlobalName) (n : Lean.Name) :
  [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([List]](#manual-List___nil) [(]](#manual-Prod___mk)Lean.Name [×]](#manual-Prod___mk) [List]](#manual-List___nil) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)[)]](#manual-Prod___mk))



[Lean.Macro.resolveGlobalName]](#manual-Lean___Macro___resolveGlobalName)
  (n : Lean.Name) :
  [Lean.MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM)
    ([List]](#manual-List___nil) [(]](#manual-Prod___mk)Lean.Name [×]](#manual-Prod___mk) [List]](#manual-List___nil) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)[)]](#manual-Prod___mk))
```

Resolves the given name to an overload list of global definitions.
The `[List]](#manual-List___nil) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)` in each alternative is the deduced list of projections
(which are ambiguous with name components).

Remark: it will not trigger actions associated with reserved names. Recall that Lean
has reserved names. For example, a definition `foo` has a reserved name `foo.def` for theorem
containing stating that `foo` is equal to its definition. The action associated with `foo.def`
automatically proves the theorem. At the macro level, the name is resolved, but the action is not
executed. The actions are executed by the elaborator when converting `Syntax` into `Expr`.

### 23.5.3. Quotation {#manual-quotation}

*Quotation* marks code for representation as data of type `[Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)`.
Quoted code is parsed, but not elaborated—while it must be syntactically correct, it need not make sense.
Quotation makes it much easier to programmatically generate code: rather than reverse-engineering the specific nesting of `[node]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)` values that Lean's parser would produce, the parser can be directly invoked to create them.
This is also more robust in the face of refactoring of the grammar that may change the internals of the parse tree without affecting the user-visible concrete syntax.
Quotation in Lean is surrounded by ``(` and `)`.

The syntactic category or parser being quoted may be indicated by placing its name after the opening backtick and parenthesis, followed by a vertical bar (`|`).
As a special case, the name `tactic` may be used to parse either tactics or sequences of tactics.
If no syntactic category or parser is provided, Lean attempts to parse the quotation both as a term and as a non-empty sequence of commands.
Term quotations have higher priority than command quotations, so in cases of ambiguity, the interpretation as a term is chosen; this can be overridden by explicitly indicating that the quotation is of a command sequence.

**Example: Term vs Command Quotation Syntax**

In the following example, the contents of the quotation could either be a function application or a sequence of commands.
Both match the same region of the file, so the [local longest-match rule]](#manual---tech-term-local-longest-match-rule) is not relevant.
Term quotation has a higher priority than command quotation, so the quotation is interpreted as a term.
Terms expect their [antiquotations]](#manual---tech-term-antiquotations) to have type `[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term` rather than `[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command`.

```lean
example (cmd1 cmd2 : [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command) : [MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command) :=
`($cmd1 $cmd2)
```

The result is two type errors like the following:

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  cmd1
has type
  [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command
but is expected to have type
  [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term
in the application
  cmd1.[raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
```

The type of the quotation (`[MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command)`) is not used to select a result because syntax priorities are applied prior to elaboration.
In this case, specifying that the antiquotations are commands resolves the ambiguity because function application would require terms in these positions:

```lean
example (cmd1 cmd2 : [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command) : [MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command) :=
`($cmd1:command $cmd2:command)
```

Similarly, inserting a command into the quotation eliminates the possibility that it could be a term:

```lean
example (cmd1 cmd2 : [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command) : [MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `command) :=
`($cmd1 $cmd2 [#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "hello!")
```

syntaxQuotations

Lean's syntax includes quotations for terms, commands, tactics, and sequences of tactics, as well as a general quotation syntax that allows any input that Lean can parse to be quoted.
Term quotations have the highest priority, followed by tactic quotations, general quotations, and finally command quotations.

```lean
term ::=
      `(term)
    | `(command+)
    | `(tactic|tactic)
    | `(tactic|tactic;*)
    | `(p:ident|Parse a p here )
```

Rather than having type `[Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)`, quotations are monadic actions with type `m [Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)`.
Quotation is monadic because it implements [hygiene]](#manual---tech-term-hygienic) by adding [macro scopes]](#manual---tech-term-macro-scopes) and pre-resolving identifiers, as described in [the section on hygiene]](#manual-macro-hygiene).
The specific monad to be used is an implicit parameter to the quotation, and any monad for which there is an instance of the `MonadQuotation` type class is suitable.
`MonadQuotation` extends `MonadRef`, which gives the quotation access to the source location of the syntax that the macro expander or elaborator is currently processing. `MonadQuotation` additionally includes the ability to add [macro scopes]](#manual---tech-term-macro-scopes) to identifiers and use a fresh macro scope for a sub-task.
Monads that support quotation include `[MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM)`, `TermElabM`, `CommandElabM`, and `TacticM`.

#### 23.5.3.1. Quasiquotation {#manual-quasiquotation}

*Quasiquotation* is a form of quotation that may contain *antiquotations*, which are regions of the quotation that are not quoted, but instead are expressions that are evaluated to yield syntax.
A quasiquotation is essentially a template; the outer quoted region provides a fixed framework that always yields the same outer syntax, while the antiquotations yield the parts of the final syntax that vary.
All quotations in Lean are quasiquotations, so no special syntax is needed to distinguish quasiquotations from other quotations.
The quotation process does not add macro scopes to identifiers that are inserted via antiquotations, because these identifiers either come from another quotation (in which case they already have macro scopes) or from the macro's input (in which case they should not have macro scopes, because they are not introduced by the macro).

Basic antiquotations consist of a dollar sign (`$`) immediately followed by an identifier.
This means that the value of the corresponding variable, which should be a syntax tree, is to be substituted into this position of the quoted syntax.
Entire expressions may be used as antiquotations by wrapping them in parentheses.

Lean's parser assigns every antiquotation a syntax category based on what the parser expects at the given position.
If the parser expects syntax category `c`, then the antiquotation's type is `[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) c`.

Some syntax categories can be matched by elements of other categories.
For example, numeric and string literals are valid terms in addition to being their own syntax categories.
Antiquotations may be annotated with the expected category by suffixing them with a colon and the category name, which causes the parser to validate that the annotated category is acceptable in the given position and construct any intermediate layers that are required in the parse tree.

syntaxAntiquotations

```lean
antiquot ::=
      $ident(:ident)?
    | $(term)(:ident)?
```

Whitespace is not permitted between the dollar sign ('$') that initiates an antiquotation and the identifier or parenthesized term that follows.
Similarly, no whitespace is permitted around the colon that annotates the syntax category of the antiquotation.

**Example: Quasiquotation**

Both forms of antiquotation are used in this example.
Because natural numbers are not syntax, `[quote]](#manual-Lean___Quote___mk)` is used to transform a number into syntax that represents it.

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
example [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m] (x : [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) (n : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) : m [Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) :=
`($x + $([quote]](#manual-Lean___Quote___mk) (n + 2)))
```

**Example: Antiquotation Annotations**

This example requires that `m` is a monad that can perform quotation.

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m]
```

By default, the antiquotation `$e` is expected to be a term, because that's the syntactic category that's immediately expected as the second argument to addition.

```lean
def ex1 (e) := show m _ from `(2 + $e)
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [ex1]](#manual-ex1-_LPAR_in-Antiquotation-Annotations_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[ex1]](#manual-ex1-_LPAR_in-Antiquotation-Annotations_RPAR_) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m] (e : [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term) : m [(]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term[)]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
```

Annotating `$e` as a numeric literal succeeds, because numeric literals are also valid terms.
The expected type of the parameter `e` changes to `TSyntax `num`.

```lean
def ex2 (e) := show m _ from `(2 + $e:num)
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [ex2]](#manual-ex2-_LPAR_in-Antiquotation-Annotations_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[ex2]](#manual-ex2-_LPAR_in-Antiquotation-Annotations_RPAR_) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m] (e : [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `num) : m [(]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term[)]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
```

Spaces are not allowed between the dollar sign and the identifier.

```lean
```lean
def ex2 (e) := show m _ from `(2 + $ e:num)
```
```

```lean
<example>:1:34-1:36: unexpected token '$'; expected '`(tactic|', 'do' or no space before spliced term
```

Spaces are also not allowed before the colon:

```lean
```lean
def ex2 (e) := show m _ from `(2 + $e :num)
```
```

```lean
<example>:1:37-1:39: unexpected token ':'; expected ')'
```

**Example: Expanding Quasiquotation**

Printing the definition of `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Expanding-Quasiquotation_RPAR_)` demonstrates the expansion of a quasiquotation.

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
def f [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m]
(x : [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) (n : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) : m [Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) :=
`(fun k => $x + $([quote]](#manual-Lean___Quote___mk) (n + 2)) + k)
#print [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Expanding-Quasiquotation_RPAR_)
```

```lean
def f : {m : Type → Type} → [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] → [Lean.MonadQuotation m] → [Lean.Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term) → [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) → m [Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) :=
fun {m} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [Lean.MonadQuotation m] x n => do
  let info ← Lean.MonadRef.mkInfoFromRefPos
  let scp ← Lean.getCurrMacroScope
  let quotCtx ← Lean.MonadQuotation.getContext
  [pure]](#manual-Pure___mk)
      [{]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
          [raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) [:=]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
            Syntax.node2 info `Lean.Parser.Term.fun ([Syntax.atom]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info "fun")
              (Syntax.node4 info `Lean.Parser.Term.basicFun
                (Syntax.node1 info `null ([Syntax.ident]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info "k".[toRawSubstring']](#manual-String___toRawSubstring___) (Lean.addMacroScope quotCtx `k scp) [[]](#manual-List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)))
                ([Syntax.node]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info `null #[]) ([Syntax.atom]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info "=>")
                (Syntax.node3 info `«term_+_»
                  (Syntax.node3 info `«term_+_» x.[raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) ([Syntax.atom]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info "+") ([Lean.quote]](#manual-Lean___Quote___mk) `term [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)).[raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk))
                  ([Syntax.atom]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info "+")
                  ([Syntax.ident]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) info "k".[toRawSubstring']](#manual-String___toRawSubstring___) (Lean.addMacroScope quotCtx `k scp) [[]](#manual-List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)))) [}]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk).[raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
```

In this output, the quotation is a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) block.
It begins by constructing the source information for the resulting syntax, obtained by querying the compiler about the current user syntax being processed.
It then obtains the current macro scope and the name of the module being processed, because macro scopes are added with respect to a module to enable independent compilation and avoid the need for a global counter.
It then constructs a node using helpers such as `Syntax.node1` and `Syntax.node2`, which create a `[Syntax.node]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)` with the indicated number of children.
The macro scope is added to each identifier, and `[TSyntax.raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)` is used to extract the contents of typed syntax wrappers.
The antiquotations of `x` and `[quote]](#manual-Lean___Quote___mk) (n + 2)` occur directly in the expansion, as parameters to `Syntax.node3`.

#### 23.5.3.2. Splices {#manual-splices}

In addition to including other syntax via antiquotations, quasiquotations can include *splices*.
Splices indicate that the elements of an array are to be inserted in order.
The repeated elements may include separators, such as the commas between list or array elements.
Splices may consist of an ordinary antiquotation with a *splice suffix*, or they may be *extended splices* that provide additional repeated structure.

Splice suffixes consist of either an asterisk or a valid atom followed by an asterisk (`*`).
Suffixes may follow any identifier or term antiquotation.
An antiquotation with the splice suffix `*` corresponds to a use of `many` or `many1`; both the `*` and `+` suffixes in syntax rules correspond to the `*` splice suffix.
An antiquotation with a splice suffix that includes an atom prior to the asterisk corresponds to a use of `sepBy` or `sepBy1`.
The splice suffix `?` corresponds to a use of `optional` or the `?` suffix in a syntax rule.
Because `?` is a valid identifier character, identifiers must be parenthesized to use it as a suffix.

While there is overlap between repetition specifiers for syntax and antiquotation suffixes, they have distinct syntaxes.
When defining syntax, the suffixes `*`, `+`, `,*`, `,+`, `,*,?`, and `,+,?` are built in to Lean.
There is no shorter way to specify separators other than `,`.
Antiquotation suffixes are either just `*` or whatever atom was provided to `sepBy` or `sepBy1` followed by `*`.
The syntax repetitions `+` and `*` correspond to the splice suffix `*`; the repetitions `,*`, `,+`, `,*,?`, and `,+,?` correspond to `,*`.
The optional suffix `?` in syntax and splices correspond with each other.

| Syntax Repetition | Splice Suffix |
| --- | --- |
| `+` `*` | `*` |
| `,*` `,+` `,*,?` `,+,?` | `,*` |
| `sepBy(_, "S")` `sepBy1(_, "S")` | `S*` |
| `?` | `?` |

**Example: Suffixed Splices**

This example requires that `m` is a monad that can perform quotation.

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m]
```

By default, the antiquotation `$e` is expected to be an array of terms separated by commas, as is expected in the body of a list:

```lean
def ex1 (xs) := show m _ from `(#[$xs,*])
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [ex1]](#manual-ex1-_LPAR_in-Suffixed-Splices_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[ex1]](#manual-ex1-_LPAR_in-Suffixed-Splices_RPAR_) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m] (xs : [Syntax.TSepArray]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___TSepArray___mk) `term ",") : m [(]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term[)]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
```

However, Lean includes a collection of coercions between various representations of arrays that will automatically insert or remove separators, so an ordinary array of terms is also acceptable:

```lean
def ex2 (xs : [Array]](#manual-Array___mk) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term)) :=
show m _ from `(#[$xs,*])
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [ex2]](#manual-ex2-_LPAR_in-Suffixed-Splices_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[ex2]](#manual-ex2-_LPAR_in-Suffixed-Splices_RPAR_) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m] (xs : [Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [(]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term[)]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)) : m [(]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `term[)]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)
```

Repetition annotations may also be used with term antiquotations and syntax category annotations.
This example is in `CommandElabM` so the result can be conveniently logged.

```lean
def ex3 (size : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) := show CommandElabM _ from [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut nums : [Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := #[]
for i in [0:size] do
nums := nums.[push]](#manual-Array___push) i
let stx ← `(#[$(nums.[map]](#manual-Array___map) ([Syntax.mkNumLit]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___mkNumLit) ∘ toString)):num,*])
-- Using logInfo here causes the syntax to be rendered via
-- the pretty printer.
logInfo stx
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [ex3]](#manual-ex3-_LPAR_in-Suffixed-Splices_RPAR_) 4
```

```lean
#[0, 1, 2, 3]
```

**Example: Non-Comma Separators**

The following unconventional syntax for lists separates numeric elements by either em dashes or double asterisks, rather than by commas.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "⟦" sepBy1(num, " — ") "⟧": term
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "⟦" sepBy1(num, " ** ") "⟧": term
```

This means that `—*` and `***` are valid splice suffixes between the `⟦` and `⟧` atoms.
In the case of `***`, the first two asterisks are the atom in the syntax rule, while the third is the repetition suffix.

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(⟦$n:num—*⟧) => `(⟦$n***⟧)
| `(⟦$n:num***⟧) => `([$n,*])
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ⟦1 — 2 — 3⟧
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[,]](#manual-List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

**Example: Optional Splices**

The following syntax declaration optionally matches a term between two tokens.
The parentheses around the nested `term` are needed because `term?` is a valid identifier.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "⟨| " (term)? " |⟩": term
```

The `?` splice suffix for a term expects an `[Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)`:

```lean
def mkStx [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m]
(e : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) : m [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term) :=
`(⟨| $(e)? |⟩)
```

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [mkStx]](#manual-mkStx-_LPAR_in-Optional-Splices_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[mkStx]](#manual-mkStx-_LPAR_in-Optional-Splices_RPAR_) {m : Type → Type} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m] [MonadQuotation m] (e : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) : m [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)
```

Supplying `[some]](#manual-Option___none)` results in the optional term being present.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) logInfo (← [mkStx]](#manual-mkStx-_LPAR_in-Optional-Splices_RPAR_) ([some]](#manual-Option___none) ([quote]](#manual-Lean___Quote___mk) 5)))
```

```lean
⟨| 5 |⟩
```

Supplying `[none]](#manual-Option___none)` results in the optional term being absent.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) logInfo (← [mkStx]](#manual-mkStx-_LPAR_in-Optional-Splices_RPAR_) [none]](#manual-Option___none))
```

```lean
⟨| |⟩
```

#### 23.5.3.3. Token Antiquotations {#manual-token-antiquotations}

In addition to antiquotations of complete syntax, Lean features *token antiquotations* which allow the source information of an atom to be replaced with the source information from some other syntax.
The resulting synthetic source information is marked [canonical]](#manual---tech-term-canonical) so that it will be used for error messages, proof states, and other feedback.
This is primarily useful to control the placement of error messages or other information that Lean reports to users.
A token antiquotation does not allow an arbitrary atom to be inserted via evaluation.
A token antiquotation consists of an atom (that is, a keyword)

syntaxToken Antiquotations

Token antiquotations replace the source information (of type `[SourceInfo]](#manual-Lean___SourceInfo___original)`) on a token with the source information from some other syntax.

```lean
antiquot ::= ...
    | atom%$ident
```

### 23.5.4. Matching Syntax {#manual-quote-patterns}

## See Also

New syntax is defined using [syntax extensions]](#manual-syntax-rules).

Quasiquotations can be used in pattern matching to recognize syntax that matches a template.
Just as antiquotations in a quotation that's used as a term are regions that are treated as ordinary non-quoted expressions, antiquotations in patterns are regions that are treated as ordinary Lean patterns.
Quote patterns are compiled differently from other patterns, so they can't be intermixed with non-quote patterns in a single [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) expression.
Like ordinary quotations, quote patterns are first processed by Lean's parser.
The parser's output is then compiled into code that determines whether there is a match.
Syntax matching assumes that the syntax being matched was produced by Lean's parser, either via quotation or directly in user code, and uses this to omit some checks.
For example, if nothing but a particular keyword can be present in a given position, the check may be omitted.

Syntax matches a quote pattern in the following cases:

Atoms
:   Keyword atoms (such as [`if`]](#manual-termIfThenElse) or [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)) result in singleton nodes whose kind is `token.` followed by the atom.
    In many cases, it is not necessary to check for specific atom values because the grammar allows only a single keyword, and no checking will be performed.
    If the syntax of the term being matched requires the check, then the node kind is compared.

    Literals, such as string or numeric literals, are compared via their underlying string representation.
    The pattern ``(0x15)` and the quotation ``(21)` do not match.

Nodes
:   If both the pattern and the value being matched represent `[Syntax.node]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)`, there is a match when both have the same syntax kind, the same number of children, and each child pattern matches the corresponding child value.

Identifiers
:   If both the pattern and the value being matched are identifiers, then their literal `Name` values are compared for equality modulo macro scopes.
    Identifiers that “look” the same match, and it does not matter if they refer to the same binding.
    This design choice allows quote pattern matching to be used in contexts that don't have access to a compile-time environment in which names can be compared by reference.

Because quotation pattern matching is based on the node kinds emitted by the parser, quotations that look identical may not match if they come from different syntax categories.
If in doubt, including the syntax category in the quotation can help.

Variables bound by syntax pattern matches are of type `[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) k`, where `k` describes the potential syntax kinds.
Variables in repetitions are of type `[TSyntaxArray]](#manual-Lean___TSyntaxArray) k`, or `[TSepArray]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___TSepArray___mk) k sep` if the repetition is separated with the string `sep`.
`[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)` is described in more detail in [the section on typed syntax]](#manual-typed-syntax).

**Example: Syntax Pattern Matching**

List comprehensions are a notation for writing lists that is inspired by standard set builder notation.
A list comprehension consists of square brackets that contain a result term followed by some nubmer of *qualifiers*; each qualifier either introduces a variable from some other list or imposes a condition that must be satisfied.
Qualifiers are nested: each new variable's value is evaluated for every prior value.

```lean
syntax qbind := ident "←" term
syntax qpred := term
syntax qualifier := atomic([qbind]](#manual-qbind-_LPAR_in-Syntax-Pattern-Matching_RPAR_)) <|> [qpred]](#manual-qpred-_LPAR_in-Syntax-Pattern-Matching_RPAR_)
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "[" term "|" [qualifier]](#manual-qualifier-_LPAR_in-Syntax-Pattern-Matching_RPAR_),* "]" : term
```

List comprehensions can be desugared to a sequence of calls to `[List.flatMap]](#manual-List___flatMap)`.
Variable introductions are translated to a `[flatMap]](#manual-List___flatMap)` on the variable's value expression, while predicates are translated to a conditional that returns one or zero values if the predicate is true or false.
The body of the final `[flatMap]](#manual-List___flatMap)` is the result term.

This desugaring can be implemented as a macro that uses quasiquotation patterns:

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(term|[$e | $qs,* ]) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let init ← `([$e])
qs.[getElems]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___TSepArray___getElems).[foldrM]](#manual-Array___foldrM) (β := [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) (init := init) fun
| `([qualifier]](#manual-qualifier-_LPAR_in-Syntax-Pattern-Matching_RPAR_)|$x ← $e'), r =>
`(($e' : List _) |>.flatMap fun $x => $r)
| `([qualifier]](#manual-qualifier-_LPAR_in-Syntax-Pattern-Matching_RPAR_)|$e':term), r =>
`(([if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) $e' [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) [()] [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) []) |>.flatMap fun () => $r)
| other, _ =>
[Macro.throwErrorAt]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwErrorAt) other "Unknown qualifier"
```

Initially, the sequence of qualifiers has type `[TSepArray]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___TSepArray___mk) `qualifier ","`, indicating that it represents a comma-separated sequence of qualifiers.
`[TSepArray.getElems]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___TSepArray___getElems)` transforms it into a `[TSyntaxArray]](#manual-Lean___TSyntaxArray) `qualifier`, which is an abbreviation for `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `qualifier)`.
This allows [generalized field notation]](#manual---tech-term-generalized-field-notation) to be used to call `[Array.foldrM]](#manual-Array___foldrM)`.
The `term` annotation in the branch for predicates is required to prevent the matched value from having syntax kind ``qualifier`; one `[node]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)` must be unwrapped from the value.

List comprehensions behave as expected:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [ s!"{x}; {y}" |
x ← (1...5).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rco___toList),
x % 2 = 0,
y ← [[true]](#manual-Bool___false), [false]](#manual-Bool___false)]
]
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"2; true"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "2; false"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "4; true"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "4; false"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

### 23.5.5. Defining Macros {#manual-defining-macros}

There are two primary ways to define macros: the [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command and the [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command.
The [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command associates a macro with existing syntax, while the [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command simultaneously defines new syntax and a macro that translates it to existing syntax.
The [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command can be seen as a generalization of [`notation`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___notation) that allows the expansion to be generated programmatically, rather than simply by substitution.

#### 23.5.5.1. The `macro_rules` Command {#manual-macro_rules}

syntaxRule-Based Macros With `macro_rules`

The [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command takes a sequence of rewrite rules, specified as syntax pattern matches, and adds each as a macro.
The rules are attempted in order, before previously-defined macros, and later macro definitions may add further macro rules.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [docComment]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___docComment)?
      ([@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)[attrInstance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attrInstance-next),*[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next))?
      attrKind macro_rules ((kind := ident))?
        (| `((p:ident|)?Suitable syntax for p ) => term)*
```

The patterns in the macros must be quotation patterns.
They may match syntax from any syntax category, but a given pattern can only ever match a single syntax kind.
If no category or parser is specified for the quotation, then it may match terms or (sequences of) commands, but never both.
In case of ambiguity, the term parser is chosen.

Internally, macros are tracked in a table that maps each [syntax kind]](#manual---tech-term-syntax-kind) to its macros.
The [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command may be explicitly annotated with a syntax kind.

If a syntax kind is explicitly provided, the macro definition checks that each quotation pattern has that kind.
If the parse result for the quotation was a [choice node]](#manual---tech-term-choice-node) (that is, if the parse was ambiguous), then the pattern is duplicated once for each alternative with the specified kind.
It is an error if none of the alternatives have the specified kind.

If no kind is provided explicitly, then the kind determined by the parser is used for each pattern.
The patterns are not required to all have the same syntax kind; macros are defined for each syntax kind used by at least one of the patterns.
It is an error if the parse result for a quotation pattern was a [choice node]](#manual---tech-term-choice-node) (that is, if the parse was ambiguous).

The documentation comment associated with [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) is displayed to users if the syntax itself has no documentation comment.
Otherwise, the documentation comment for the syntax itself is shown.

As with [notations]](#manual-notations) and [operators]](#manual-operators), macro rules may be declared `scoped` or `local`.
Scoped macros are only active when the current namespace is open, and local macro rules are only active in the current [section scope]](#manual---tech-term-section-scope).

**Example: Idiom Brackets**

Idiom brackets are an alternative syntax for working with applicative functors.
If the idiom brackets contain a function application, then the function is wrapped in `[pure]](#manual-Pure___mk)` and applied to each argument using `<*>`.
Lean does not support idiom brackets by default, but they can be defined using a macro.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) (name := idiom) "⟦" (term:[arg]](#manual-precArg))+ "⟧" : term
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(⟦$f $args*⟧) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut out ← `(pure $f)
for arg in args do
out ← `($out <*> $arg)
return out
```

This new syntax can be used immediately.

```lean
def addFirstThird [[Add]](#manual-Add___mk) α] (xs : [List]](#manual-List___nil) α) : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) α :=
⟦[Add.add]](#manual-Add___mk) xs[0]? xs[2]?⟧
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [addFirstThird]](#manual-addFirstThird-_LPAR_in-Idiom-Brackets_RPAR_) (α := [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) []
```

```lean
[none]](#manual-Option___none)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [addFirstThird]](#manual-addFirstThird-_LPAR_in-Idiom-Brackets_RPAR_) [1]
```

```lean
[none]](#manual-Option___none)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [addFirstThird]](#manual-addFirstThird-_LPAR_in-Idiom-Brackets_RPAR_) [1,2,3,4]
```

```lean
[some]](#manual-Option___none) 4
```

**Example: Scoped Macros**

Scoped macro rules are active only in their namespace.
When the namespace `ConfusingNumbers` is open, numeric literals will be assigned an incorrect meaning.

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) ConfusingNumbers
```

The following macro recognizes terms that are odd numeric literals, and replaces them with double their value.
If it unconditionally replaced them with double their value, then macro expansion would become an infinite loop because the same rule would always match the output.

```lean
scoped [macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `($n:num) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if n.[getNat]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___getNat) % 2 = 0 then [Lean.Macro.throwUnsupported]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwUnsupported)
let n' := (n.[getNat]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___getNat) * 2)
`($([Syntax.mkNumLit]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___mkNumLit) (info := n.[raw]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk).getHeadInfo) (toString n')))
```

Once the namespace ends, the macro is no longer used.

```lean
end ConfusingNumbers
```

Without opening the namespace, numeric literals function in the usual way.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3, 4)
```

```lean
[(]](#manual-Prod___mk)3[,]](#manual-Prod___mk) 4[)]](#manual-Prod___mk)
```

When the namespace is open, the macro replaces `3` with `6`.

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) ConfusingNumbers
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3, 4)
```

```lean
[(]](#manual-Prod___mk)6[,]](#manual-Prod___mk) 4[)]](#manual-Prod___mk)
```

It is not typically useful to change the interpretation of numeric or other literals in macros.
However, scoped macros can be very useful when adding new rules to extensible tactics such as `[trivial]](#manual-trivial)` that work well with the contents of the namespaces but should not always be used.

Behind the scenes, a [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command generates one macro function for each syntax kind that is matched in its quote patterns.
This function has a default case that throws the `[unsupportedSyntax]](#manual-Lean___Macro___Exception___unsupportedSyntax)` exception, so further macros may be attempted.

A single [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command with two rules is not always equivalent to two separate single-match commands.
First, the rules in a [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) are tried from top to bottom, but recently-declared macros are attempted first, so the order would need to be reversed.
Additionally, if an earlier rule in the macro throws the `[unsupportedSyntax]](#manual-Lean___Macro___Exception___unsupportedSyntax)` exception, then the later rules are not tried; if they were instead in separate [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) commands, then they would be attempted.

**Example: One vs. Two Sets of Macro Rules**

The `arbitrary!` macro is intended to expand to some arbitrarily-determined value of a given type.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) (name := arbitrary!) "arbitrary! " term:[arg]](#manual-precArg) : term
```

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! ()) => `(())
| `(arbitrary! Nat) => `(42)
| `(arbitrary! ($t1 × $t2)) => `((arbitrary! $t1, arbitrary! $t2))
| `(arbitrary! Nat) => `(0)
```

Users may extend it by defining further sets of macro rules, such as this rule for `[Empty]](#manual-Empty)` that fails:

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! Empty) => [throwUnsupported]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwUnsupported)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) arbitrary! (Nat × Nat)
```

```lean
[(]](#manual-Prod___mk)42[,]](#manual-Prod___mk) 42[)]](#manual-Prod___mk)
```

If all of the macro rules had been defined as individual cases, then the result would have instead used the later case for `[Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)`.
This is because the rules in a single [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command are checked from top to bottom, but more recently-defined [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) commands take precedence over earlier ones.

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! ()) =>
`(())
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! Nat) =>
`(42)
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! ($t1 × $t2)) =>
`((arbitrary! $t1, arbitrary! $t2))
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! Nat) =>
`(0)
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! Empty) =>
[throwUnsupported]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwUnsupported)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) arbitrary! (Nat × Nat)
```

```lean
[(]](#manual-Prod___mk)0[,]](#manual-Prod___mk) 0[)]](#manual-Prod___mk)
```

Additionally, if any rule throws the `[unsupportedSyntax]](#manual-Lean___Macro___Exception___unsupportedSyntax)` exception, no further rules in that command are checked.

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! (List Nat)) => [throwUnsupported]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwUnsupported)
| `(arbitrary! (List $_)) => `([])
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! (Array Nat)) => `(#[42])
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(arbitrary! (Array $_)) => [throwUnsupported]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwUnsupported)
```

The case for `[List]](#manual-List___nil) [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)` fails to elaborate, because macro expansion did not translate the `arbitrary!` syntax into something supported by the elaborator.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) arbitrary! (List Nat)
```

```lean
elaboration function for `arbitrary!` has not been implemented
  arbitrary! (List Nat)
```

The case for `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)` succeeds, because the first set of macro rules are attempted after the second throws the exception.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) arbitrary! (Array Nat)
```

```lean
[#[]](#manual-List___toArray)42[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)
```

#### 23.5.5.2. The `macro` Command {#manual-macro-command}

The [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command simultaneously defines a new [syntax rule]](#manual---tech-term-syntax-rules) and associates it with a [macro]](#manual---tech-term-Macros).
Unlike [`notation`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___notation), which can define only new term syntax and in which the expansion is a term into which the parameters are to be substituted, the [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command may define syntax in any [syntax category]](#manual---tech-term-syntax-categories) and it may use arbitrary code in the `[MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM)` monad to generate the expansion.
Because macros are so much more flexible than notations, Lean cannot automatically generate an unexpander; this means that new syntax implemented via the [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command is available for use in *input* to Lean, but Lean's output does not use it without further work.

syntaxMacro Declarations

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [docComment]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___docComment)?
      ([@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)[attrInstance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attrInstance-next),*[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next))?
      attrKind macro(:prec)? ((name := ident))? ((priority := prio))? macroArg* : ident =>
        macroRhs
```

syntaxMacro Arguments

A macro's arguments are either syntax items (as used in the [`syntax`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) command) or syntax items with attached names.

```lean
macroArg ::=
    stx
```

```lean
macroArg ::= ...
    | ident:stx
```

In the expansion, the names that are attached to syntax items are bound; they have type `[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk)` for the appropriate syntax kinds.
If the syntax matched by the parser does not have a defined kind (e.g. because the name is applied to a complex specification), then the type is `[TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) Name.anonymous`.

The documentation comment is associated with the new syntax, and the attribute kind (none, `local`, or `scoped`) governs the visibility of the macro just as it does for notations: `scoped` macros are available in the namespace in which they are defined or in any [section scope]](#manual---tech-term-section-scope) that opens that namespace, while `local` macros are available only in the local section scope.

Behind the scenes, the [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) command is itself implemented by a macro that expands it to a [`syntax`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) command and a [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command.
Any attributes applied to the macro command are applied to the syntax definition, but not to the [`macro_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) command.

#### 23.5.5.3. The Macro Attribute {#manual-macro-attribute}

[Macros]](#manual---tech-term-Macros) can be manually added to a syntax kind using the [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___macro) attribute.
This low-level means of specifying macros is typically not useful, except as a result of code generation by macros that themselves generate macro definitions.

attributeThe `macro` Attribute

The [`macro`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___macro) attribute specifies that a function is to be considered a [macro]](#manual---tech-term-Macros) for the specified syntax kind.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | macro ident
```

**Example: The Macro Attribute**

```lean
/-- Generate a list based on N syntactic copies of a term -/
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) (name := rep) "[" num " !!! " term "]" : term
@[[macro]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___macro) [rep]](#manual-rep-_LPAR_in-The-Macro-Attribute_RPAR_)]
def expandRep : Macro
| `([ $n:num !!! $e:term]) =>
let e' := [Array.replicate]](#manual-Array___replicate) n.[getNat]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___getNat) e
`([$e',*])
| _ =>
[throwUnsupported]](#manual-Lean___Macro___throwUnsupported)
```

Evaluating this new expression demonstrates that the macro is present.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [3 !!! "hello"]
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"hello"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "hello"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "hello"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

---



## Notations and Macros — 23.6. Elaborators {#manual-notations-and-macros-236-elaborators}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Elaborators/

## See Also

- Elaborators process [new syntax extensions]](#manual-syntax-ext).
- [Quotation patterns]](#manual-quote-patterns) are the most typical way to destructure syntax.

While macros allow Lean to be extended by translating new syntax into existing syntax, *elaborators* allow the new syntax to be processed directly.
Elaborators have access to everything that Lean itself uses to implement each feature of the language.
Defining a new elaborator allows a language extension to be just as powerful as any built-in feature of Lean.

Elaborators come in two varieties:

- *Command elaborators* are used to add new commands to Lean.
  Commands are implemented as side effects: they may add new constants to the global environment, extend compile-time tables such as the one that tracks [instances]](#manual---tech-term-instances), they can provide feedback in the form of information, warnings, or errors, and they have full access to the `[IO]](#manual-IO)` monad.
  Command elaborators are associated with the [syntax kinds]](#manual---tech-term-kind) that they can handle.
- *Term elaborators* are used to implement new terms by translating the syntax into Lean's core type theory.
  They can do everything that command elaborators can do, and they additionally have access to the local context in which the term is being elaborated.
  Term elaborators can look up bound variables, bind new variables, unify two terms, and much more.
  A term elaborator must return a value of type `Lean.Expr`, which is the AST of the core type theory.

This section provides an overview and a few examples of elaborators.
Because Lean's own elaborator uses the same tools, the source code of the elaborator is a good source of further examples.
Just like macros, multiple elaborators may be associated with a syntax kind; they are tried in order, and elaborators may delegate to the next elaborator in the table by throwing the `[unsupportedSyntax]](#manual-Lean___Macro___Exception___unsupportedSyntax)` exception.

syntaxElaboration Rules

The [`elab_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules) command takes a sequence of elaboration rules, specified as syntax pattern matches, and adds each as an elaborator.
The rules are attempted in order, before previously-defined elaborators, and later elaborators may add further options.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | [docComment]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___docComment)?
      ([@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)[attrInstance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attrInstance-next),*[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next))?
      attrKind elab_rules ((kind := ident))? (: ident)? (<= ident)?
        (| `((p:ident|)?Suitable syntax for p ) => term)*
```

Commands, terms, and tactics each maintain a table that maps syntax kinds to elaborators.
The syntax category for which the elaborator should be used is specified after the colon, and must be `term`, `command`, or `tactic`.
The [`<=`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules) binds the provided identifier to the current expected type in the context in which a term is being elaborated; it may only be used for term elaborators, and if present, then `term` is implied as the syntax category.

attributeElaborator Attribute

Elaborators can be directly associated with syntax kinds by applying the appropriate attributes.
Each takes the name of a syntax kind and associates the definition with the kind.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | term_elab (prio
       | ident)
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | command_elab (prio
       | ident)
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | tactic (prio
       | ident)
```

### 23.6.1. Command Elaborators {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Elaborators--Command-Elaborators}

A command elaborator has type `CommandElab`, which is an abbreviation for `[Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) → CommandElabM [Unit]](#manual-Unit)`.
Command elaborators may be implicitly defined using [`elab_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules), or explicitly by defining a function and applying the `command_elab` attribute.

**Example: Querying the Environment**

A command elaborator can be used to query the environment to discover how many constants have a given name.
This example uses `getEnv` from the `MonadEnv` class to get the current environment.
`Environment.constants` yields a mapping from names to information about them (e.g. their type and whether they are a definition, [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types) declaration, etc).
`logInfoAt` allows informational output to be associated with syntax from the original program, and a [token antiquotation]](#manual---tech-term-token-antiquotations) is used to implement the Lean convention that output from interactive commands is associated with their keyword.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "#count_constants " ident : command
[elab_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules) : command
| `(#count_constants%$tok $x) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let pattern := x.[getId]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___getId)
let env ← getEnv
let mut count : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 0
for (y, _) in env.constants do
if pattern.isSuffixOf y then
count := count + 1
logInfoAt tok m!"Found {count} instances of '{pattern}'"
```

```lean
def interestingName := 55
def NS.interestingName := "Another one"
#count_constants interestingName
```

```lean
Found 2 instances of 'interestingName'
```

### 23.6.2. Term Elaborators {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Elaborators--Term-Elaborators}

A term elaborator has type `TermElab`, which is an abbreviation for `[Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) → [Option]](#manual-Option___none) Expr → TermElabM Expr`.
The optional `Expr` parameter is the type expected for the term being elaborated, which is `none` if no type is yet known.
Like command elaborators, term elaborators may be implicitly defined using [`elab_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules), or explicitly by defining a function and applying the `term_elab` attribute.

**Example: Avoiding a Type**

This examples demonstrates an elaborator for syntax that is the opposite of a type ascription.
The provided term may have any type *other* than the one indicated, and metavariables are solved pessimistically.
In this example, `elabType` invokes the term elaborator and then ensures that the resulting term is a type.
`Meta.inferType` infers a type for a term, and `Meta.isDefEq` attempts to make two terms [definitionally equal]](#manual---tech-term-definitional-equality) by unification, returning `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if it succeeds.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) (name := notType) "(" term " !: " term ")" : term
@[term_elab [notType]](#manual-notType-_LPAR_in-Avoiding-a-Type_RPAR_)]
def elabNotType : TermElab := fun stx _ => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let `(($tm:term !: $ty:term)) := stx
| throwUnsupportedSyntax
let unexpected ← elabType ty
let e ← elabTerm tm [none]](#manual-Option___none)
let eTy ← Meta.inferType e
if (← Meta.isDefEq eTy unexpected) then
throwErrorAt tm m!"Got unwanted type {eTy}"
else [pure]](#manual-Pure___mk) e
```

If the type position does not contain a type, then `elabType` throws an error:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([1, 2, 3] !: "not a type")
```

```lean
type expected, got
  ("not a type" : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray))
```

If the term's type is definitely not equal to the provided type, then elaboration succeeds:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([1, 2, 3] !: [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray))
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[,]](#manual-List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

If the types match, an error is thrown:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (5 !: [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero))
```

```lean
Got unwanted type [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
```

The type equality check may fill in missing information, so `sorry` (which may have any type) is also rejected:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (sorry !: [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray))
```

```lean
Got unwanted type [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)
```

**Example: Using Any Local Variable**

Term elaborators have access to the expected type and to the local context.
This can be used to create a term analogue of the `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)` tactic.

The first step is to access the local context using `getLocalHyps`.
It returns the context with the outermost bindings on the left, so it is traversed in reverse order.
For each local assumption, a type is inferred with `Meta.inferType`.
If it can be equal to the expected type, then the assumption is returned; if no assumption is suitable, then an error is produced.

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "anything!" : term
[elab_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules) <= expected
| `(anything!) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let hyps ← getLocalHyps
for h in hyps.[reverse]](#manual-Array___reverse) do
let t ← Meta.inferType h
if (← Meta.isDefEq t expected) then return h
throwError m!"No assumption in {hyps} has type {expected}"
```

The new syntax finds the function's bound variable:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (fun (n : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) => 2 + anything!) 5
```

```lean
7
```

It chooses the most recent suitable variable, as desired:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
let x := "x"
let y := "y"
"It was " ++ y
```

```lean
"It was y"
```

When no assumption is suitable, it returns an error that describes the attempt:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
let x := [Nat.zero]](#manual-Nat___zero)
let y := "hello"
fun (f : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) → [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) =>
(anything! : [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat) → [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat))
```

```lean
No assumption in [x, y, f] has type [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat) → [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat)
```

Because it uses unification, the natural number literal is chosen here, because numeric literals may have any type with an `[OfNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk)` instance.
Unfortunately, there is no `[OfNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk)` instance for functions, so instance synthesis later fails.

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
let x := 5
let y := "hello"
(anything! : [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat) → [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat))
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) ([Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat) → [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat)) 5
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `5` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat) → [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat)
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

### 23.6.3. Custom Tactics {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Elaborators--Custom-Tactics}

Custom tactics are described in the [section on tactics]](#manual-custom-tactics).

---



## Notations and Macros — 23.7. Extending `do`-Notation {#manual-notations-and-macros-237-extending--notation}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Extending--do--Notation/

Macros and elaborators can be used to extend Lean with new commands and terms.
In addition, [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-notation can be extended.
Extensions to [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-notation define new kinds of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements.
Macros translate the new [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements into previously existing [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements, while elaborators have access to more information and can produce arbitrary terms in Lean's type theory.

This chapter describes the extension mechanisms that are available for [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-notation.
Extensible [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-notation was introduced in Lean version 4.29.0; prior to this release, it was not extensible.
The extensible [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) elaborator is controlled by the option `[backward.do.legacy]](#manual-backward___do___legacy)`, which defaults to `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`:

option

```lean
backward.do.legacy
```

Default value: `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`

Use the legacy `do` elaborator instead of the new, extensible implementation.

When `[backward.do.legacy]](#manual-backward___do___legacy)` is `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`, the extensible elaborator is enabled.
Custom [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element elaborators extend the desugaring described in [the section on syntax for monads]](#manual-do-notation).

### 23.7.1. Elaboration Overview {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Extending--do--Notation--Elaboration-Overview}

The [syntax kind]](#manual---tech-term-syntax-kind) `doElem` represents individual [`do`-elements]](#manual---tech-term-do-elements).
A sequence of these elements is represented by the syntax kind `doSeq`, which makes up the body of a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-block.
The elaborator for [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) invokes a specialized elaboration framework on the `doSeq` in its body, elaborating each `doElem` in turn.
This specialized framework allows each element in the sequence to modify the elaboration of subsequent elements, as well as to track information such as enclosing loops (for `break` and `continue`), the way to escape via `return`, and the set of mutable variables.

Elaboration of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements is very similar to that of terms.
First, if the syntax in question is a [macro]](#manual---tech-term-Macros), then it is expanded.
This is repeated until the result of macro expansion is no longer a macro.
Next, an internal table is consulted to find the elaboration procedure associated with the [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element's syntax kind.
This table is separate from the table of term elaborators, because [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element elaborators have a different type.
If a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element consists only of a term, then the Lean parser wraps it in the syntax kind `doExpr`; its elaborator invokes the term elaborator, ensuring that the term has the correct type for the [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-block.

### 23.7.2. Macros in `do`-Notation {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Extending--do--Notation--Macros-in--do--Notation}

Macro expansion occurs during the elaboration of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements.
There is no fundamental difference between [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element macros and term or command macros; they are distinguished by being defined for syntax that is part of the `doElem` syntax category.

**Example: Multi-Way if**

As an alternative to a nested sequence of `if`-terms, this “multi-way `if`” places each condition at the same syntactic level:

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) (name := multiIfTerm)
"if " withPosition(
(colGe atomic("|" (atomic(ident " : "))? term) " => " term)+
colGe "|" " else " " => " term
) : term
```

It is [indentation-sensitive]](#manual-syntax-indentation).
It can be implemented as a recursive macro that emits the expected nested `if`:

```lean
def mkTermIf (h? : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Ident]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Ident)) (g b e : [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) : [MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) h? [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [some]](#manual-Option___none) h => `([if]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) $h:ident : $g [then]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) $b [else]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) $e)
| [none]](#manual-Option___none) => `([if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) $g [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) $b [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) $e)
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(if | $[$h?:ident :]? $g:term => $b:term | else => $e:term) =>
[mkTermIf]](#manual-mkTermIf-_LPAR_in-Multi-Way--if_RPAR_) h? g b e
| `(if | $[$h?:ident :]? $g:term => $b:term
| $[$h2?:ident :]? $g2:term => $b2:term
$[| $[$hs?:ident :]? $gs:term => $bs:term]*
| else => $e:term) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[mkTermIf]](#manual-mkTermIf-_LPAR_in-Multi-Way--if_RPAR_) h? g b
(← `(if | $[$h2?:ident :]? $g2 => $b2
$[| $[$hs?:ident :]? $gs => $bs]*
| else => $e))
```

It can be used like any other term:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
let sign : [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat) → [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) := fun n =>
if
| n < 0 => "neg"
| n = 0 => "zero"
| else => "pos"
(sign (-2), sign 0, sign 5)
```

```lean
[(]](#manual-Prod___mk)"neg"[,]](#manual-Prod___mk) "zero"[,]](#manual-Prod___mk) "pos"[)]](#manual-Prod___mk)
```

This macro can be adapted to be a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element by placing it in the `doElem` syntax category and replacing each arm of the multi-way `if` with a `doSeq` instead of a `[Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)`.
The syntax definition is almost the same; however, the `else` branch is optional:

```lean
[syntax]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) (name := multiIf)
"if " withPosition(
(colGe atomic("|" (atomic(ident " : "))? term) " => " doSeq)+
(colGe "|" " else " " => " doSeq)?
) : doElem
```

Likewise, a helper function to attach the optional condition hypothesis name to `if` is useful:

```lean
def mkDoIf (h? : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Ident]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Ident)) (g : [Term]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___Term)) (b : [TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) ``doSeq)
(els? : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) ``doSeq)) : [MacroM]](#manual-Lean___MacroM) ([TSyntax]](#manual-Lean___TSyntax___mk) `doElem) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) h? [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [some]](#manual-Option___none) h =>
`(doElem| if $h : $g then $b $[else $els?]?)
| [none]](#manual-Option___none) =>
`(doElem| if $g then $b $[else $els?]?)
```

The implementation as a recursive macro is also nearly the same:

```lean
[macro_rules]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(doElem| if | $[$h?:ident :]? $g:term => $b:doSeq
$[| else => $e:doSeq]?) =>
[mkDoIf]](#manual-mkDoIf-_LPAR_in-Multi-Way--if_RPAR_) h? g b e
| `(doElem| if | $[$h?:ident :]? $g:term => $b:doSeq
| $[$h2?:ident :]? $g2:term => $b2:doSeq
$[| $[$hs?:ident :]? $gs:term => $bs:doSeq]*
$[| else => $e:doSeq]?) => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[mkDoIf]](#manual-mkDoIf-_LPAR_in-Multi-Way--if_RPAR_) h? g b <| [some]](#manual-Option___none)
(← `(doSeq| if | $[$h2?:ident :]? $g2 => $b2
$[| $[$hs?:ident :]? $gs => $bs]*
$[| else => $e]?))
```

It can be used in [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do):

```lean
def getEven : [IO]](#manual-IO) { n : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) // n % 2 = 0 ∨ n % 3 = 0} := [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let n ← (← [IO.getStdin]](#manual-IO___getStdin)).[getLine]](#manual-IO___FS___Stream___mk)
let [some]](#manual-Option___none) n := n.[toNat?]](#manual-String___toNat___)
| [throw]](#manual-MonadExcept___mk) <| [IO.userError]](#manual-IO___userError) s!"Not a Nat: {n}"
if
| h : n % 2 = 0 =>
[IO.println]](#manual-IO___println) s!"{n} is even."
return ⟨n, [.inl]](#manual-Or___inl) h⟩
| h : n % 3 = 0 =>
[IO.println]](#manual-IO___println) s!"{n} is divisible by 3."
return ⟨n, [.inr]](#manual-Or___inl) h⟩
| else =>
[throw]](#manual-MonadExcept___mk) <| [IO.userError]](#manual-IO___userError) s!"Invalid input {n}"
```

#### 23.7.2.1. Limitations {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Extending--do--Notation--Macros-in--do--Notation--Limitations}

When an extension can be implemented as a macro, it is usually best to do so.
Macros are much simpler to maintain, and they inherit bug fixes from the implementation of the syntax that they expand to.
However, macros cannot implement all possible extensions:

- They cannot access information about the set of mutable variables, nor can they override it.
- They cannot implement novel control structures that are not expressible in terms of built-in control structures.
- They cannot place a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-sequence into some new context (such as underneath a binder) while keeping it as part of the enclosing [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-block for the purposes of early return and mutable variables.

In these cases, it may be necessary to define an elaborator.

**Example: Freezing Mutable Variables with a Macro**

Within a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) block, new `let` bindings may not shadow existing `let mut` bindings.
However, many mutable variables are not modified after they are initialized.
It might be convenient to indicate this fact by removing their mutability.

There is no existing way to replace a mutable variable with an immutable one, so this feature can't be implemented with a macro that expands to an existing [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element which makes the variable immutable for the remainder of the block.
However, the operator can be structured so that it introduces a scope in which the mutable variable is immutable by expanding to a function call:

```lean
[macro]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___macro) "freeze " x:ident " in " body:doSeq : doElem =>
`(doElem| (fun $x => [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) $body) $x)
```

While it may seem promising, this macro-based solution has severe drawbacks.
First, the body of the resulting function constitutes a new [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-block.
This means that mutable variables in the surrounding block cannot be modified:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Id.run]](#manual-Id___run) [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 0
x := x + 1
let mut y := 0
freeze x in
y := 2 * x
return y
```

```lean
Variable `y` cannot be mutated. Only variables declared using `let mut` can be mutated.
      If you did not intend to mutate but define `y`, consider using `let y` instead
```

Additionally, an early `return` exits the inner [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do), rather than the surrounding one, as indicated by the fact that it is expected to return a `[Unit]](#manual-Unit)` (in this case, the universe-polymorphic `[PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)`):

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Id.run]](#manual-Id___run) [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 0
x := x + 1
let mut y := 0
freeze x in
return x
return y
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  x
has type
  [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
but is expected to have type
  [PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)
```

### 23.7.3. Elaboration {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Extending--do--Notation--Elaboration}

Elaboration of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements occurs in the `DoElabM` monad.
This monad is a wrapper around `TermElabM` that provides one extra [reader]](#manual-reader-monad) value: a [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elaboration context.
The elaborators also receive an additional argument: a description of the elaboration *continuation*.
The continuation represents the remainder of the [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-block, after the current element; it includes both a `DoElabM` action that will elaborate the remainder of the block and the name by which that term will refer to the result of the current elaboration step.
Unlike term elaborators, which return the elaborated term to a surrounding elaboration context, [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element elaborators invoke the provided continuation to arrange for the elaboration of the rest of the [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-block.

Elaborators are associated with syntax kinds using the `doElem_elab` attribute.
They should have type `[DoElab]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElab)`.
In addition to an elaborator, each custom [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element that's implemented via an elaborator must be provided with [control information]](#manual-do-elab-control-info).

def

```lean
[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElab]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElab) : Type



[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElab]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElab) : Type
```

The type of elaborators for `do` block elements.

It is `elabTerm `([do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) $e; $rest) = elabDoElem e dec`, where `elabDoElem e ·` is the elaborator for
`do` element `e`, and `dec` is the `DoElemCont` describing the elaboration of the rest of the block
`rest`.

attributeDo Element Elaborators

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | doElem_elab
```

Registers a `do` element elaborator for the given syntax node kind.

A `do` element elaborator should have type `DoElab` (which is
`[Lean.Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing) → DoElemCont → DoElabM Expr`), i.e. should take syntax of the given syntax node kind
and a `DoElemCont` as parameters and produce an expression.

When elaborating a `do` block `do e; rest`, the elaborator for `e` is invoked with the syntax of `e`
and the `DoElemCont` representing `rest`.

The `elab_rules` and `elab` commands should usually be preferred over using this attribute
directly.

Additionally, [`elab_rules`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___elab_rules) can be used to simultaneously define an elaborator and associate it with syntax.
Just as `elab_rules : term <= ty` binds the expected type to `ty`, `elab_rules : doElem <= dec` binds the continuation to `dec`.

Just as term elaborators may recursively invoke elaboration on their sub-terms by calling functions such as `elabTerm`, [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element elaborators may elaborate nested [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements or sequences of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements.
To elaborate a single [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-element, call `[elabDoElem]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___elabDoElem)`.
To elaborate a non-empty array of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements, call `[elabDoElems1]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___elabDoElems1)`.
To elaborate a sequence of [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elements, call `[elabDoSeq]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___elabDoSeq)`.

#### 23.7.3.1. Monad Operations {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Extending--do--Notation--Elaboration--Monad-Operations}

The elaboration framework provides several helpers that make it more convenient and efficient to construct applications of the current monad and its operations.

#### 23.7.3.2. Continuations {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Notations-and-Macros--Extending--do--Notation--Elaboration--Continuations}

A [`do`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)-elaboration continuation consists of an elaborator that is waiting for the result of the present element together with metadata such as the type that this result is expected to have.

structure

```lean
[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk) : Type



[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk) : Type
```

Elaboration of a `do` block `[do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) $e; $rest`, results in a call
`elabTerm `([do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do) $e; $rest) = elabDoElem e dec`, where `elabDoElem e ·` is the elaborator for `do`
element `e`, and `dec` is the `DoElemCont` describing the elaboration of the rest of the block
`rest`.

If the semantics of `e` resumes its continuation `rest`, its elaborator must bind its result to
`resultName`, ensure that it has type `resultType` and then elaborate `rest` using `dec`.

Clearly, for term elements `e : m α`, the result has type `α`.
More subtly, for binding elements `[let]](#manual-let) x := e` or `let x ← e`, the result has type `[PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)` and is
unrelated to the type of the bound variable `x`.

Examples:

- `return` drops the continuation; `return x; pure ()` elaborates to `pure x`.
- `let x ← e; rest x` elaborates to `e >>= fun x => rest x`.
- `let x := 3; let y ← (let x ← e); rest x` elaborates to
  `let x := 3; e >>= fun x_1 => let y := (); rest x`, which is immediately zeta-reduced to
  `let x := 3; e >>= fun x_1 => rest x`.
- `one; two` elaborates to `one >>= fun (_ : PUnit) => two`; it is an error if `one` does not have
  type `[PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)`.

Constructor

```lean
[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemCont.mk]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)
```

Fields

```lean
resultName : Name
```

The name of the monadic result variable.

```lean
resultType : Expr
```

The type of the monadic result.

```lean
k : Elab.Do.DoElabM Expr
```

The continuation to elaborate the `rest` of the block. It assumes that the result of the `do`
block is bound to `resultName` with the correct type (that is, `resultType`, potentially refined
by a dependent `[match]](#manual-match)`).

```lean
kind : [Elab.Do.DoElemContKind]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemContKind___nonDuplicable)
```

Whether we are OK with generating the code of the continuation multiple times, e.g. in different
branches of a `[match]](#manual-match)` or `[if]](#manual-if)`.

inductive type

```lean
[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemContKind]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemContKind___nonDuplicable) : Type



[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemContKind]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemContKind___nonDuplicable) : Type
```

`duplicable` allows for more optimizations.

Many elaborators require that the continuation is expecting a particular type for its result.
It is very common, for example, for an elaborator to result in `[Unit]](#manual-Unit)` if it returns no result.
Checking the type at an earlier stage can result in better error messages:

def

```lean
[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemCont.ensureUnit]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___ensureUnit) (dec : [Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)) :
  Elab.Do.DoElabM [Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)



[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemCont.ensureUnit]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___ensureUnit)
  (dec : [Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)) :
  Elab.Do.DoElabM [Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)
```

Given a continuation `dec`, returns a continuation derived from `dec` with result type `[PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)`.
If `dec` already has result type `[PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)`, simply returns `dec`. Otherwise, an error is logged and a
new continuation is returned that calls `dec` with `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)` as a result.

  (ref : [Syntax]](#manual-Lean___Syntax___missing)) : Elab.Do.DoElabM [Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)

  Elab.Do.DoElabM [Elab.Do.DoElemCont]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___mk)
```

If `dec` already has result type `[PUnit]](#manual-PUnit___unit)`, simply returns `dec`. Otherwise, an error is logged and a

[Lean.Elab.Do.DoElemCont.ensureHasTypeAt]](#manual-Lean___Elab___Do___DoElemCont___ensureHasTypeAt)
